name: composite-view
intent: Compose one page from independent, reusable view fragments: a layout template declares the fixed regions, self-contained subviews fill them, and a view manager decides which fragment goes where and when - at translation time or per request - so layout policy and page content are managed separately and shared markup is defined exactly once.
problem: Page markup is duplicated: every view repeats the header, navigation, footer and list-row markup, so a layout change must be edited in many files and the copies drift apart. Content and layout cannot be changed independently, fragments owned by different teams cannot be released separately, and per-fragment access control or caching has no unit to attach to. The trigger is that several pages share regions or repeated row markup - or a page must be assembled from content owned by different teams or data sources - and nothing combines modular, atomic portions of a view into a composite whole.
context: Server-side presentation layers that render complete HTML pages: template-engine stacks (JSP/Jakarta Pages, Thymeleaf, Twirl, Leaf, Django/Jinja, Razor, Rails ActionView, EJS/Pug/Handlebars, Go html/template) as well as typed HTML DSLs and component functions (kotlinx.html, Twirl, JSX/TSX). It applies when layout consistency across many pages matters, when regions repeat across pages (chrome, navigation, teasers, table rows), and when fragments are owned or reused independently; fragment caching, page caching and HTMX-style partial responses all build on it. On the client side, React (children, render props, compound components) and Vue (slots, scoped slots) provide browser-native mechanisms for the same composition discipline.
benefits: Shared markup lives in exactly one fragment: a change to the navigation, footer or teaser markup propagates to every page that includes it, instead of being repeated per view.
Pages become compositions: the layout declares named regions and the page decides which fragment fills each one, so new pages reuse existing pieces rather than copying them.

Atomic fragments are reusable across pages and contexts - the same product row, user card or error banner serves many pages, appears in different positions, and may be nested inside another composite view.

Fragments are independent work units with a narrow interface, so designers, backend authors and separate teams can prototype static placeholders and then substitute real content without touching the whole page.
Layout policy is managed separately from content: mixed static and dynamic fragments can be included side by side, and whole pages or individual fragments become cacheable units.

On client-side component frameworks (React, Vue), slots/children enable runtime composition of independently-authored UI pieces without a shared build step, enabling progressive enhancement and independent deployment of UI modules.
tradeoffs: Runtime overhead is the documented price of flexibility: each fragment is resolved, parsed/cached and rendered per request, so deep fragment nesting multiplies per-request work unless parsed templates or whole pages are cached.

More artifacts and indirection to maintain than one inline page - layout, fragments, composition wiring and the engine's configuration all have to be understood before the output can be reasoned about.

Fragments commonly inherit ambient context (Thymeleaf fragment expressions, EJS locals, Handlebars partial context, Rails instance variables, Django's non-`only` include), which creates hidden data dependencies that break the moment the fragment is reused on another page.

Fragment and layout references are stringly typed in most engines (include paths, fragment expressions, partial names), so a rename fails at render time rather than at compile time - only compile-time template systems (Askama, Twirl, Razor, typed component functions) turn that into a build error.

Over-fragmentation: dozens of one-line fragments and deep include chains make the rendered page hard to trace, and duplicated markup migrates from the pages into competing fragments instead of disappearing.

Escaping and inclusion become security-relevant: whether a fragment is escaped depends on the engine's output directive, and a fragment name or path built from request data turns dynamic inclusion into template injection or local-file disclosure.
Client-side composition (React/Vue) shifts rendering cost to the browser and adds reconciliation overhead for deeply nested slot hierarchies, which can hurt Time-to-Interactive on low-end devices.
Scoped slots (Vue) and render props (React) create implicit data-flow dependencies that are harder to trace than explicit props, making the fragment boundary guarantees of the pattern leak.

participants.responsibility: The aggregate view: defines the page structure - shared shell plus named regions (placeholders) in a fixed order - and owns the overall look and feel, independently of the content that fills the regions.
One atomic, reusable piece of the page (navigation, teaser, product row, footer) that renders itself from declared inputs; it may itself be composite and include further subviews.

Manages inclusion of fragments into the composite view: resolves each fragment reference, decides conditionally which fragments appear (roles, system state, configuration), and passes the model or parameter scope; it is the engine's include facility or a helper/custom-tag layer above it.
Supplies the model for the page and hands off to the composite view; it does not know the page's internal fragment structure beyond the layout it selects.

The concrete primitive that renders a fragment in place - include directive or action, fragment expression, partial call, {{template}}/{% include %}, or DSL function call - including resolution rules, parameter passing and escaping. In client-side frameworks, this role is filled by children props (React), slot/consumer mechanisms (Vue), or outlet components (Angular).

use_cases: Portal-style pages that combine independently owned feeds (news, weather, quotes, profile panes) into one seamless page whose layout is managed separately from the content.
A consistent site shell across a large page set: header, navigation, breadcrumbs, footer and sidebars rendered from single fragments instead of copies per page.
List and table pages where one row fragment is rendered once per record (Rails collection partials, Django include in a loop, Go {{template}} inside {{range}}, Razor <partial> in a foreach).
Multi-channel presentation where the same fragments feed different layouts or channels (web page, email body, HTMX partial response) without rewriting the content markup.
Form and error presentation where label, field and validation-summary fragments are reused across many forms.
Migrating a legacy view layer incrementally: extract the duplicated chrome first as fragments, then decompose the page body region by region.

Vue named slots: a page-level layout component declares slot outlets (header, sidebar, default) and child components or page templates fill each slot, enabling independent authoring of shell and content.

React children composition: a compound UI component (e.g., a data table) accepts heterogeneous child fragments and composes them into its structure without prop-drilling, keeping the table's internal layout policy separate from its cell content.

HTMX partial responses: a server endpoint returns only the fragment that needs to be replaced (a row, a form, a notification), treating the fragment as an independent composable unit that can be served standalone or embedded.

Email templating: a transactional email system uses a layout fragment (logo, footer, color scheme) with content fragments specific to each email type, so branding changes propagate without touching email copy.

Apache Tiles: a template JSP exposes named attributes (title, header, menu, body, footer) and tiles.xml definitions bind each attribute to a concrete fragment; definitions nest and extend, and a view preparer fills the model before render - the reference implementation of the View Manager role.

Shopify Online Store 2.0 themes: JSON templates and section groups list which section fragments compose a page, each section declaring a {% schema %} of settings and nestable blocks, so merchants add, remove and reorder fragments without touching Liquid - composition driven by data, not code.

Hugo static sites: baseof.html declares a named region with {{ block "main" . }} and page templates fill it with {{ define "main" }}, while header/footer land chrome and partials fill repeated regions; the whole composed tree is rendered once at build time, which is also why fragment caching is pointless there.
avoid_when: A single small page or a throwaway script: one template that renders it directly is simpler than a layout plus fragments.
The markup is not actually shared and the page is short - composition machinery then only adds indirection.
Presentation is fundamentally a programmatic translation of domain data rather than a template with holes: a Transform View or plain markup-rendering functions express that directly.
Output is identical across requests: pre-generate it once (Page Cache) instead of composing fragments on every request.
Fragments would each need most of the ambient context (no narrow interfaces): fix the fragment boundaries or use component objects with explicit inputs before adopting the mechanism.
The framework already owns composition in a way you cannot extend (a CMS template system or a fixed page builder) - do not rebuild the roles on top.
Deep slot hierarchies on the client: if a component's slot content itself declares slots, the resulting component tree becomes hard to trace and debug; a flat prop interface is preferable.
anti_patterns: "Reuse" that copies the header and footer into every template and calls it modular: the duplication the pattern exists to remove is still there, just named.
Fragments that reach into ambient context (session, request, controller instance variables, ViewBag) for half their inputs, so they render correctly on one page and subtly wrong on the next.
Dynamic fragment selection driven by unvalidated request input, letting the caller pick an arbitrary template path (template injection, local file disclosure).
Fragment explosion: dozens of one-line fragments in deep include chains where a single readable template used to be, to the point that the composed page can no longer be traced.
The same region rendered by two competing fragments depending on the caller, so the layout consistency the pattern promises is lost again.

Prop drilling through multiple composite layers instead of using slots or context: the parent mediates every piece of data that a deeply nested fragment needs, coupling layers that the pattern meant to keep independent.
design_principles: DRY: shared markup is defined once and included, never copied per page.
Separation of concerns: layout (structure) is managed independently of fragment content and of the data that fills it.
Single responsibility: each fragment owns one atomic piece of presentation and is unaware of the pages that include it.
Explicit interfaces (information hiding): a fragment declares the parameters it needs rather than reading ambient state.
Open/closed: new pages and regions are added by composing existing fragments, not by editing shared templates.
Least privilege for fragment access: only the data explicitly passed to a fragment should be visible inside it; ambient context should never be implicitly available.
best_practices: Give every reusable fragment an explicit parameter interface (locals:, with ... only, {{> p k=v}}, fragment arguments, typed props) instead of relying on inherited context.
Keep logic out of the layout: it declares regions and shared shell markup; conditional composition belongs in the view manager or the page's model.

Keep fragment references static where the engine allows it (compile-time templates in Askama/Twirl/Razor, literal paths in EJS/Pug/Leaf); never build an include name from request input without an allow-list.
Escape by default and treat raw/unescaped output directives (EJS <%- %>, Thymeleaf th:utext, Leaf #raw, template.HTML) as explicit, reviewed exceptions.
Cache at the right level: parse templates once per process, prefer compiled templates, and cache whole pages (Page Cache) where the composed output repeats.
Test fragments in isolation (component/partial render helpers) and the assembled page with an integration test; a fragment rename should fail in CI, not in production.
Name fragments by role and keep one owner per region so the same markup never lives in two fragments that can drift apart.
Use strict/typed locals (Rails `strict_locals:`, Vue `defineProps`, React `PropTypes` or TypeScript interfaces) to catch missing or extra fragment inputs at build time, not render time.
In Vue, prefer scoped slots for data-dependent composition but keep slot content itself simple; deeply nested slot composition is a code-smell equivalent to fragment explosion.
In React, prefer explicit composition (children) over render props for simple cases; reserve render props for genuinely optional or swap-able rendering logic.
Maintain an allow-list of permitted fragment paths for any dynamic fragment resolution; never accept a full filesystem path or user-supplied string as a fragment identifier without validation.

For HTMX-driven partial responses, design each partial endpoint to be self-contained (include its own necessary data, not rely on page-level state) so it behaves identically when served standalone or as part of a full page.
pitfalls: Template injection via dynamic fragment names: CVE-2025-1686 (Pebble) and Django path-traversal vulnerabilities both stem from fragment/path resolution accepting unsanitized user input. Always validate against an allow-list or enum of permitted fragment names.

Ambient context leaking into fragments: when a fragment implicitly reads request-scoped or session-scoped data, it works in the context where it was developed but silently fails when reused in a different rendering context (e.g., an async HTMX request that lacks the original request context).

Parse-time template caching with deep nesting: compiling a deeply nested fragment tree on first request can cause a thundering-herd problem on cache expiry; warm the template cache proactively or use fine-grained per-fragment caching.

Client-side reconciliation cost: React's virtual DOM reconciles every child in a slot; a page with 100 list items each wrapped in a slot-capable component pays O(n) diffing overhead that a single flat render loop avoids.
Slot vs. prop confusion in team codebases: developers mix slot usage with prop drilling, creating two competing composition idioms in the same component library that confuse consumers.

Hot-reload and composition: in development, template changes to a fragment used in many pages may not invalidate the composed output unless the layout template itself is also touched, leading to stale renders during iterative development.

Wrong move: stacking base templates three or more extends levels deep, redefining the same blocks at each level -> failure: the rendered page can only be traced by walking the whole chain, and overriding a parent block silently drops nested child blocks (Django ticket #7324) -> instead: cap inheritance at two levels (base + section base) and compose the rest with flat includes/partials that take explicit parameters.

Wrong move: fragment-cache a fragment that varies per user or session because the engine offers a cache tag -> failure: personalized markup leaks across users or the cache key degenerates so every request misses -> instead: split the region into a cacheable public fragment plus a small per-user fragment, or make every varying key part of the explicit cache key.

Wrong move: reach for scope-copying inclusion primitives (Liquid {% include %}) so fragments can see the caller's variables -> failure: the fragment silently depends on ambient names and the per-call scope copy costs measurable render time -> instead: use isolated-scope inclusion with named parameters (Liquid {% render %}, Django {% include ... only %}, Rails partial locals).
sources: Alur, Crupi & Malks, Core J2EE Patterns: Best Practices and Design Strategies (2nd ed., 2003) - Composite View (presentation tier): a view composed of atomic, dynamically included subviews, managed by a View Manager.

Oracle, Core J2EE Patterns - Composite View: context, forces, participants (Composite View, View Manager, Included View) and the runtime-overhead tradeoff, https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/composite-view.html
Java Design Patterns catalog, Composite View, https://java-design-patterns.com/patterns/composite-view

Fowler, Martin. Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (PoEAA). Wiley, 2002. Composite View entry in the catalog at https://martinfowler.com/eaaCatalog, alongside Two-Step View which applies a separate transformation step to apply layout, and Transform View for programmatic data translation.
Vue.js, Slots documentation - named slots, scoped slots and default slot composition as a client-side manifestation of the Composite View pattern, https://vuejs.org/guide/components/slots
React, Composition vs Inheritance - children prop and render props as the React idiom for fragment composition, https://legacy.reactjs.org/docs/composition-vs-inheritance.html

Rails Guides, Layouts and Rendering in Rails - ActionView partials (render :partial), collection rendering, and strict_locals for explicit fragment interfaces, https://guides.rubyonrails.org/layouts_and_rendering.html

HTMX, Server Examples and Partial Rendering - treating HTML fragments as self-contained composable units served via htmx-requested endpoints, https://htmx.org/docs and https://htmx.org/server-examples

SentinelOne, CVE-2025-1686: Pebble Templates Path Traversal Flaw (Jan 2026) - documents the template injection class of vulnerability that affects dynamic fragment name resolution in template engines, https://www.sentinelone.com/blog/pebble-templates-path-traversal-flaw-cve-2025-1686

Core J2EE Patterns (online edition), Composite View - purpose, reasons for use, and the view-management strategies (JavaBean, standard/custom tag, transformer, early/late-binding resource), http://corej2eepatterns.com/Patterns2ndEd/CompositeView.htm

Apache Tiles, The Composite View Pattern and Tiles Concepts - template with fillable attributes, definitions, nested/extending definitions and view preparers as the framework realization of the View Manager, https://tiles.apache.org/framework/tutorial/pattern.html and https://tiles.apache.org/framework/tutorial/basic/concepts.html

Shopify Themes, Snippets and Sections architecture - {% render %} with named parameters, isolated snippet scope, and JSON templates/section groups composing merchant-editable section fragments, https://shopify.dev/docs/storefronts/themes/architecture/snippets and https://shopify.dev/docs/storefronts/themes/architecture/sections

Hugo, Template Types and Partial Decorators - baseof.html blocks filled by define actions, partials for repeated regions, and with + templates.Inner decorators that wrap inner content in reusable containers, https://gohugo.io/templates/types/ and https://gohugo.io/templates/partial-decorators/

Augment Code, Django Template Best Practices for Enterprise Teams - criticism of deep extends/block chains: unreadable inheritance graphs, merge conflicts and duplication migrating into parent templates; recommends a two-level inheritance cap plus shared includes, https://www.augmentcode.com/guides/django-template-best-practices-for-enterprise-teams

Django ticket #7324, block.super with nested block statements - concrete evidence that multi-level block override semantics are underspecified and silently drop nested blocks, https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/7324
